items.title: 5.5 Elastic deformation, plastic deformation and elastic limit

source_refs.note: Topic 5.5 with Fig. 5.5 and Example 5.1 (PDF 98-99, printed 95-96). The Brain Teaser on the floating steel ship is carried in 5.7.

blocks.text: In a tensile test a metal wire is extended at a specified deformation rate, and the stresses generated in the wire during deformation are continuously measured by a suitable electronic device fitted in the mechanical testing machine. A force-elongation diagram or stress-strain curve is plotted automatically on an X-Y chart recorder; a typical stress-strain curve for a ductile material is shown in Fig. 5.5.

blocks.alt: A graph of Stress (sigma) against Strain from the origin O. The curve rises as a straight line from O to A, bends through B, rises more slowly to its highest point C and then falls to D, where it ends. A, B and C are marked with small circles.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.5: Stress-strain curve of a typical ductile material (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.5).

blocks.text: In the initial stage of deformation the stress increases linearly with the strain until point A on the curve, the proportional limit (sigma_p), defined as the greatest stress a material can endure without losing straight-line proportionality between stress and strain. Hooke's law, which states that the strain (deformation) is directly proportional to the stress (force or load), is obeyed in the region OA. From A to B stress and strain are not proportional.

blocks.title: Elastic limit
blocks.text: If the load is removed at any point between O and B, the curve is retraced and the material returns to its original length; in the region OB the material is said to be elastic. Point B is the yield point, and the value of stress at B is the elastic limit sigma_e.

If the stress is increased beyond the yield stress or elastic limit, the specimen becomes permanently changed and does not recover its original shape or dimension after the stress is removed. This behaviour is called plasticity; the region of plasticity is the portion of the curve from B to C. Point C represents the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) sigma_u of the material, the maximum stress a material can withstand, which can be regarded as the nominal strength of the material. Once point C is crossed the material breaks at point D, corresponding to the fracture stress sigma_f.

blocks.title: Ductile and brittle substances
blocks.text: Substances which undergo plastic deformation until they break are ductile substances, for example lead, copper and wrought iron. Substances which break just after the elastic limit is reached are brittle substances, for example glass and high-carbon steel; beryllium, bismuth and chromium are also brittle metals.

blocks.title: Example 5.1
blocks.text: A steel wire 12 mm in diameter is fastened to a log and pulled by a tractor; the length of wire between the log and the tractor is 11 m and a force of 10 000 N is required to pull the log. Calculate the stress in the wire. Solution: tensile stress sigma = F/A = 10 000 N / (3.14 x (6 x 10^-3 m)^2) = 88.46 x 10^6 N m^-2 = 88.46 MPa.
